wu: Festival Bingo: Students receive bingo cards with pictures of different festivals (Eid, Independence Day, Christmas, etc.). Teacher calls out names, students mark the pictures. First to get a line shouts 'Bingo!' and names the festivals they marked.
wuAlt: Guess the Festival: Teacher describes a festival (e.g., 'It's in November, people celebrate independence, there are parades'), students guess the name. Then students take turns describing Moroccan festivals for others to guess.
Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking 'Have you ever celebrated [festival]?' and find classmates who have, writing their names.
pres: Teacher shows a photo of a Moroccan Independence Day celebration and a US Independence Day celebration. Elicits vocabulary like 'parade', 'flag', 'speech', 'family gathering'. Models sentences: 'In Morocco, we celebrate on November 11th. In the US, they celebrate on July 4th.' Asks checking questions: 'When do we celebrate?' 'What do we see?'
presAlt: Festival Comparison Chart: On the board, draw two columns. Students call out words to fill it for Eid and Independence Day (food, clothes, activities).
Realia Display: Teacher brings in items for a celebration (Moroccan flag, US flag, a small plate of mint tea, a small piece of baklava) and elicits vocabulary and uses for each.
prac: Festival Photo Pairs: Students work in pairs. Each pair gets two photos (one Moroccan festival, one American festival). They use the model sentences to compare them: 'This is Eid. We eat couscous. This is Thanksgiving. They eat turkey.' Teacher monitors and helps with pronunciation.
pracAlt: Match the Words: Students get a worksheet with festival vocabulary (parade, flag, speech, music) and pictures. They draw lines to match the words.
Sentence Builders: Students get sentence strips with the structure '[Country] celebrates [festival] on [date]. They eat [food].' They arrange the strips to make correct sentences.
ls: Listen and Order: Students listen to a short audio recording of two people making small talk at a festival. They have a jumbled list of sentences (e.g., 'Great food, isn't it?', 'Have you been to the parade before?'). They listen and put the sentences in the correct order to make a conversation.
re: Stand Up, Sit Down: Teacher says a statement about festivals (e.g., 'You like parades.'). Students who agree stand up, students who disagree sit down. Teacher says statements using 'By 1956, Morocco had...' to reactivate the past perfect.
prod: Small Talk Elevator Game: Students are in pairs. They pretend to be in an elevator at a festival. They have 30 seconds to make small talk using the openers: 'Nice day for a festival, isn't it?', 'Have you been to this before?', 'What's your favorite part?'. They swap partners and repeat with a new topic.
rw: Reading and Writing: Students read a short text (5-6 sentences) about the history of Moroccan Independence Day. Then, they write 3 small-talk questions they could ask someone at a celebration, e.g., 'Do you like the music?', 'Is this your first time here?', 'What do you usually do on this day?'
st: Teacher tells a short, personal story about a memorable celebration, using simple past tense. Then, the class says goodbye together: 'Today we learned to compare celebrations and make small talk. Thank you, everyone. Have a good day.'
g: Students act out a festival (e.g., waving a flag, eating) and others guess.
In pairs, students have two similar festival pictures and take turns asking questions to find five differences.
Students sit in two lines. They have 1 minute to ask small talk questions, then one line moves.
Teacher asks questions like 'When is Independence Day?' 'What color is the Moroccan flag?' Students answer in teams.
Teacher says a prompt like '1956', students race to say a sentence like 'By 1956, Morocco had become independent.'
diff: Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence frame to write their small talk questions: 'Do you like ___?' 'What is ___?'
hw: Write 5 sentences in the past perfect about Moroccan history (e.g., 'By 1956, Morocco had gained its independence.')
Interview a family member about their favorite celebration and write down 3 things they said.
Write down 3 small talk questions you could ask a tourist at a festival in Morocco.
tip: Connect the lesson to students' lives by explicitly linking the language of comparison and small talk to their goals of interacting with tourists or international visitors at the American Space.
